name: Serer religion
areas: Tekrur and the Senegal River valley
the Serers living here refuse War Jabi's forced conversion and Sharia law around 1030 to 1035, and leave south
Serer lamanic authorities are in place when Mandinka migrants enter in the late 14th century; many still follow the Serer religion here, and the Xooy ceremony gathers thousands at Fatick
routes: Serers move south from Tekrur and the Senegal River valley into the Siin and Saluum valleys (from around the 11th century)
marks: Lamane Jegan Joof founded the village around the 11th century; the Raan festival is held here each April.
The Serer king of Sine, Kumba Ndoffene Famak Joof, defeated and killed Maba Diakhou Bâ here on 18 July 1867.
notes: Serers move south from the Senegal River valley from around the 11th century; Lamane Jegan Joof founds the village of Tukar around the 11th century, and around 1030 to 1035 Serers in Tekrur refuse forced conversion to Islam.
In the late 14th century Mandinka migrants enter Sine and meet Serers who already have lamanic authorities and their shrines.
In the 19th century the Serers fight Islamic marabout movements: a jihad targets them in 1861 and the king of Sine defeats Maba Diakhou Bâ in 1867; French forces conquer Senegal in 1887.

Conversion to Islam accelerates after colonisation, about 40% of Serers by the early 1910s and about 85% by the 1990s; many in Sine keep the Serer religion, and the old funeral rites of the kings of Sine are last held on 8 March 1969.
